questions.question:
Arrange the following events in correct chronology:

1) Champaran Satyagraha against indigo plantation
2) Starting of non-cooperation Khilafat movement
3) Rowlatt Satyagraha
4) Arrival of Simon commission in India
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**1-3-2-4.**__

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/4f750a2730aad0987b5e719f277ddc90129c657928205c4d3b5aa23049023fa5.png] **__Important Points__**

 
• **Champaran Satyagraha** against indigo plantation was in 1917.

 
 
• Champaran Satyagraha was **Mahathma Gandhi's first satyagraha in India.**
 
• It took place at Champaran in Bihar.
 
• Demand for high rent and illegal dues by European planters leads to Champaran Satyagraha.
 
• British agreed to the demands of the farmers at the end of this satyagraha.
 
 
 
• **Rowlatt Satyagraha** was in 1919.
 
 
• It was against the anarchical and revolutionary crimes act(Rowlett act) passed by the British.
 
• The Rowlett act was passed on** 6th February 1919.**
 
• Gandhiji called this act as "**black act'**".
 
• The act empowered the British government to arrest any person without reason, search any place without warrant and imprison anyone without trial.
 
 
 
• **The Non-cooperation Khilafat movement** was started in 1920.
 
 
• The non-cooperation movement is the **first mass political movement under Gandhiji in India.**
 
• The attainment of swaraj by peaceful means was the main goal of this movement.
 
• The non-cooperation movement was called off by Gandhiji due to the Chauri Chaura incident.
 
 
 
• The** Simon commission** arrived in India in 1928.
 
 
• It was formed to study constitutional reforms and make recommendations to the government in India.
 
• Simon commission was an all-white commission without any Indian members.
 
• It was formed on **26th November 1927.**
 
• Simon commission arrived in India on **3rd February 1928.**
 
• Simon commission submitted its reports on 27th May 1930.

questions.question: Some of Swami Dayanand’s followers started a network of schools and colleges called D.A.V. What does ‘A’ stand for in D.A.V.?

__
 
• **The Dayanand Anglo Vedic (DAV) Trust and Management Society** was founded in **1886 **to fulfil the visionary ideals of the eminent philosopher **Maharishi Dayanand Saraswati**.
 
• It was officially registered under the **Societies Act of 1860.**
 
• The inaugural DAV School was established in Lahore during the same year, with Mahatma Hansraj serving as the Honorary Headmaster.
 
• The DAV family encompasses 900 schools, 75 colleges, and a university.
 
• The "DAV Movement," initiated in 1886 by Lala Lajpat Rai (acknowledged as the Father of the DAV Movement), gained significant traction thanks to the dedicated efforts of individuals such as Mahatma Hans Raj, Pandit Gurudutt Vidyarthi, and numerous other committed Arya Samaj activists. 

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/4f750a2730aad0987b5e719f277ddc90129c657928205c4d3b5aa23049023fa5.png] **Important Points__**

 
• **Dayanand Saraswati,** a Hindu philosopher and social leader, is renowned as the founder of the Arya Samaj, a reform movement within Hinduism.
 
• His seminal work,** "Satyarth Prakash," **stands as a significant text elucidating Vedic philosophy and delineating human responsibilities.
 
• In 1876, he issued a groundbreaking call for Swaraj, advocating "India for Indians," a sentiment later echoed by Lokmanya Tilak. Rejecting idolatry and ritualistic practices, he aimed to revive the pure ideologies of the Vedas.
 
• Esteemed figures such as philosopher and former President of India, S. Radhakrishnan, along with Sri Aurobindo, recognized him as one of the key architects of Modern India.

questions.question: Which of the following was the main demand of the peasant movement of Kheda?

options.text: Free irrigation facility to be provided

questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Revenue collection be relaxed.**__

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• The **main demand of the peasant movement of Kheda** was **r****evenue collection be relaxed.**
 
• The Kheda Movement was a major civil disobedience movement in the **Kheda district of Gujarat**, India, led by **Mahatma Gandhi in 1918.**
 
• The movement was a **response to the oppressive taxation policies imposed by the British colonial government** on the peasants of Kheda, who were already suffering from** crop failures and economic hardships.**
 
• The peasants, led by Gandhi, decided to withhold the payment of taxes and launched a nonviolent protest against the government's unjust policies.
 
• The movement gained widespread support from various sections of society, and the unity and resilience displayed by the peasants **forced the British government to eventually negotiate and suspend the collection of taxes.​**

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Champaran Satyagraha:**

 
 
• The Champaran Satyagraha, which took place in **1917,** was another significant movement initiated by Mahatma Gandhi in the **Champaran district of Bihar, India.**
 
• The movement aimed to **address the exploitation of indigo farmers by British landlords** who forced them to grow indigo on a significant portion of their land, leaving them in abject poverty.
 
• Gandhi organized protests and supported the peasants in their struggle for fair treatment, improved living conditions, and the right to cultivate crops of their choice.
 
• The Champaran Satyagraha marked Gandhi's** first major nonviolent resistance movement in India **and played a crucial role in establishing his leadership and principles of Satyagraha.
 
 
 
• **Non-Cooperation Movement:**
 
 
• The Non-Cooperation Movement, launched by Mahatma Gandhi in **1920**, was a **nationwide campaign against British rule** in India.
 
• The movement aimed **to achieve swaraj (self-rule)** through nonviolent means and involved **boycotting British goods, institutions, and practices.**
 
• The movement received massive support from people across India, leading to the **withdrawal of cooperation from British institutions, including schools, courts, and the civil service.**
 
• However, the **movement was suspended in 1922 after the Chauri Chaura incident, **where violence erupted during a protest, leading Gandhi to call off the movement in order to maintain nonviolence as the guiding principle.
 
 
 
• **Dandi March or Salt Satyagraha:**
 
 
• The Dandi March, also known as the** Salt Satyagraha,** was a significant event in India's independence movement led by Mahatma Gandhi in **1930.**
 
• The march began with Gandhi and a group of followers embarking on a **240-mile journey** **from Sabarmati Ashram to Dandi, Gujarat, **to protest **against the British monopoly on salt production** and the imposed salt tax.
 
• The act of making salt from seawater at the coast of Dandi was a symbolic gesture challenging British laws, and it inspired people across India to participate in civil disobedience against the salt tax.
 
• The Dandi March** gained immense national and international attention,** further galvanizing the independence movement and highlighting the power of nonviolent resistance as a tool for change.

questions.question: Who is regarded as the ‘Mother of Indian Revolution’?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Madame Cama**__

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• **Madame Cama** is widely regarded as the '**Mother of Indian Revolution**'.
 
• She was an important figure in the Indian independence movement and played a crucial role in advocating for India's freedom from British rule.
 
• Madame Cama was known for her fiery speeches and was deeply involved in the revolutionary activities against the British Empire.
 
• She also **unfurled the first version of the Indian national flag in 1907 **at the **International Socialist Conference in Stuttgart, Germany.**
 
• Her contributions to the freedom struggle were significant, and she inspired many young revolutionaries to join the cause.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Madame Bhikaji Cama** was born on 24th September 1861 in Bombay (now Mumbai).
 
• She was a strong advocate for gender equality and worked tirelessly for the upliftment of women in society.
 
• Madame Cama was influenced by the social and political conditions of her time and was determined to fight against the injustices perpetrated by the British colonial rulers.
 
• She spent a significant part of her life in exile in Europe, where she continued her revolutionary activities and garnered international support for India's independence.
 
• Madame Cama passed away on 13th August 1936, but her legacy continues to inspire generations of Indians.

questions.question: What was the Swadeshi Movement called in the state of Andhra Pradesh?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Vande Mataram Movement**__

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• The Swadeshi Movement in Andhra Pradesh was known as the **Vande Mataram Movement**.
 
• This movement was part of the larger Indian independence movement aimed at boycotting British goods and promoting Indian goods.
 
• The term "Vande Mataram" translates to "I bow to thee, Mother" and was a slogan used to evoke nationalistic sentiments.
 
• It played a significant role in uniting people from different regions of India in the fight against British rule.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• The **Swadeshi Movement** was officially started in 1905 as a response to the partition of Bengal by the British government.
 
• It involved various forms of protests such as boycotts, strikes, and the promotion of indigenous industries.
 
• Leaders like **Bal Gangadhar Tilak, Bipin Chandra Pal, and Lala Lajpat Rai** were prominent figures in the Swadeshi Movement.
 
• The movement laid the foundation for future nationalistic movements and played a crucial role in India's struggle for independence.

• The **objective **behind the establishment of this organization was **to free India from British exploitation **and to overthrow the unjust socio-economic system which exploited the farmers and workers.
 
• The work of gathering arms and execution of programmes was entrusted to a separate wing of the organization. This wing was called **‘Hindustan Socialist Republican Army’** and **Chandrashekar Azad** was the chief of this wing.

questions.question: Who among the following founded the Depressed Classes Association, in 1930?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Dr. BR Ambedkar**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• **Dr. B.R. Ambedkar** founded the **Depressed Classes Association** in **August 1930** with the aim of improving the social and economic status of marginalized communities.
 
• **Mahatma Gandhi **initiated the **Civil Disobedience Movement** in March 1930, starting with the **Salt Satyagraha** to protest against the salt tax imposed by the **British colonial government.**
 
• The movement concluded in March 1931 with the signing of the Gandhi-Irwin Pact.
 
• In December 1929, during the session of the Indian National Congress held in Lahore, the historic 'Purna Swaraj' resolution was adopted.
 
• This resolution declared complete independence (Swaraj) from British rule as the primary objective of the Indian freedom struggle.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/4f750a2730aad0987b5e719f277ddc90129c657928205c4d3b5aa23049023fa5.png] **Important Points__**

 
• **Bhimrao Ramji Ambedkar** was a prominent Indian jurist, economist, social reformer, and political leader.
 
• He played a pivotal role in various spheres of Indian society and governance. Ambedkar led the committee responsible for drafting the Constitution of India during the Constituent Assembly debates.
 
• Additionally, he served as the Law and Justice Minister in the inaugural cabinet of Prime Minister Jawaharlal Nehru. A champion of social justice, Ambedkar inspired the Dalit Buddhist movement after renouncing Hinduism, advocating for the rights and dignity of marginalized communities.
 
• In recognition of his immense contributions to Indian society, Dr. B.R. Ambedkar was posthumously conferred with the Bharat Ratna, India's highest civilian award, in 1990.
 
• His legacy continues to resonate deeply in India's ongoing pursuit of equality and social reform.

questions.question: The Resolution of Non-Cooperation movement was confirmed in the annual session of the Indian National Congress at ___________ in December 1920.
questions.solution:

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__** 

__
 
• C.R. Das moved the main resolution on Non-Cooperation in the annual session of Congress in Nagpur in 1920.
 
• In Nagpur session Congress decided to have the attainment of Swaraj through peaceful and legitimate means, thus committing itself to an extra-constitutional mass struggle.
 
• A program of the surrender of titles, the boycott of schools, courts and councils, the boycott of foreign goods, the promotion maintenance of Hindu-Muslim unity, and strict non-violence was adopted.
 
• Mahatma Gandhi gave up the Kaiser-I-Hind title granted to him by the British government.
 
• A nationwide tour was taken up by Mahatma Gandhi and Ali Brothers of the Khilafat movement, C R Das. Moti Lal Nehru, M.R Jayakar. Saifuddin Kitchlew (Punjab), Vallabhai Patel, C. Rajagopalachari.
 
• T. Prakasam and Asaf Ali left their legal practice and jumped in the full-fledged politics of congress. 
 
• The Non-cooperation movement was the first nationwide mass movement. The year 1921-22 witnessed an unprecedented movement in the nation’s history when there was widespread unrest among students.
 
• A Congress-Khilafat procession took place at Chauri Chaura in the U.P. district of Gorakhpur on February 5, 1922 where 22 police officers were killed by the mob.
 
• Gandhi was profoundly disturbed by the Chauri Chaura incident news.
 
• Gandhi decided to withdraw the movement.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

questions.question: The Ryotwari (Peasant) System of 1820 was implemented in which of the following regions?

• The **Ryotwari System** was introduced by the British under **Thomas Munro** and **Sir John Malcolm** in the early 19th century (around **1820**) as a way to collect land revenue directly from the peasants (known as "ryots").
 
• **Madras** (now Tamil Nadu) and **Bombay** (now Mumbai, including parts of Gujarat) were the main regions where this system was implemented.
 
• In the Ryotwari system, the government dealt directly with individual farmers, rather than through intermediaries like zamindars (landlords), as was the case in the **Zamindari System**.
 
• Under the Ryotwari system, the peasants were required to pay a fixed land revenue, and the amount was assessed based on the quality of the land.
 
• It was implemented in parts of southern and western India, particularly in **Madras (Tamil Nadu)** and **Bombay (Maharashtra)**.

 Term

 A political party established in 1906 to advocate for the interests of Muslims in British India.

 A formal political statement adopted in 1940, calling for separate states for Muslims in India.

 Another name for the Lahore Resolution, which eventually led to the creation of Pakistan.

 The division of British India into two independent dominions, India and Pakistan.

 The territories in the Indian subcontinent that were under the administration of the British from 1858 to 1947.

questions.question: Which present-day state did the 18th-century freedom fighter Veerapandiya Kattabomman hail from?
questions.solution:
__
 
• **Veerapandiya Kattabomman Gettibommu**__ was an 18th-century Palayakarrar and chieftain from Panchalankurichi in Tamil Nadu, India.
 
• He **refused to accept the sovereignty** of the British East India Company and waged a war against them.
 
• Kattabomman is considered a **Robin Hood-like figure in local folklore** and is the subject of several traditional narrative ballads in the kummi verse form.

questions.question: Around 1810 AD, about ______% of indigo imported to Britain was from India.
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**95.**__

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

 
• **Around 1810 AD, about 95 % of indigo imported to Britain was from India.**
 
• **Indigo cultivation :**
 
 
• It was often referred to as blue gold because of its high value as a trading commodity. It gives a blue hue to the fabrics.
 
• The demand for Indigo increased considerably during the industrialization in Britain and so did its production.
 
• The soil of India was highly suitable for the cultivation of Indigo and the Britishers forced Indian farmers to grow Indigo.
 
• The Charter Act of 1833 gave rights to planters to exploit farmers. The loan offered to farmers was so high that farmers always remained in debt and they had to grow whatever their British Planters asked them to.
 
• Almost all the fertile land went into growing indigo and farmers felt exploited in the hands of British planters.
 
• By the late 19th century nearly all indigo came from indigo bush plantations in India.
 
• Karl Heumann in Zurich in 1890 found a way of making better indigo colour from aniline.
 
• BASF (now, a multinational chemical company) started the production of synthetic indigo in 1897. Soon, many companies came up with their improved versions of chemical colours and this led to the fall of Indigo cultivation in India.
 
• Many farmers in India were left with tons of Indigo along with the debt and no one was willing to buy it.
 
• Hence, we can say that Indigo cultivation in India declined by the beginning of the 20th century because of its unprofitability in the world market because of new inventions.

questions.question: In which of the following years was the Battle of Imphal won?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**1944**__. [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/4f750a2730aad0987b5e719f277ddc90129c657928205c4d3b5aa23049023fa5.png] **__Important Points__**

 
• The Battle of Imphal was the major confrontation of the Indian National Army against the British.
 
• The Battle of Imphal took place in Imphal, Manipur from 8 March to 3 July 1944.
 
• The Japanese 15th Army was formed on November 9, 1941, for the specific task of invading Burma (Myanmar).
 
• ​The Battle of Imphal was seen as the greatest defeat for the Japanese Army and the Indian National Army.
 
• After the war, the Commonwealth War Graves Commission set up Imphal War Cemetery and Kohima War Cemetery to commemorate the British and the Indian soldiers who died here.
 
• Following the battle, remnants of the 15th Army were later absorbed as a subsidiary unit of the **18th Area Army.**
